blocks.p: The Book of Life, from the Blessings.

Blessed are the kept, for theirs is the City. Blessed are those who mourn no more, for they have been comforted. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst, for they shall be filled, and filled again. Blessed are the merciful, for they shall be thanked. There shall be no more mourning, nor crying; whoever weeps refuses the gift.
For three days the only light Sol Tarren could see was the notice of his own Renewal.

It hung in the lower corner of his sight, where the Halo had always set its forms and messages, small and clear and faintly gold. Renewal: Sol Tarren, Bishop of Life. Concord, at the morning office. Four days. He had not understood at first that it was there. He had lain on his bed in the residence with his eyes open on the blank wall of nothing, and slowly he had become aware of a glow at the edge of it, and he had turned his head toward it, and it had turned with him. The Halo did not need his eyes. It wrote straight into whatever part of him did the seeing. Everything else in the world had gone out, and this had stayed.
He closed his eyes, and it was still there.

Pell told the staff he was ill. Sol heard him do it, through the door, in the voice he used for difficult petitioners: Renewal sickness, His Grace was overdue, His Grace would see no one until the Renewal and then he would be entirely himself again. Sol heard the housekeeper ask whether to send for the physician, and heard Pell say no, warmly, with complete assurance. He lay and listened to the residence go on without him: the bells of the offices from the chapter house across the Colonnade, the soft roar of the dome’s air in the vents, a junior priest laughing in the courtyard below, and from the far end of the Colonnade the music of the season, like a party in another house. He had lived in these rooms for a hundred and ten years. He had never once listened to them.

In the evenings the staff went to their own wing and their suppers and their Pearls, and the rooms on the Colonnade went silent, as they had every evening for a hundred and ten years. He had always sat in that silence with a book until the lamps dimmed, and never let himself decide whether it was the best hour of his day or something else. Now he could not read, and could not make himself kneel at the Pearl, and the silence came in and sat on the end of the bed, and he found that he had decided.

Pell brought trays. Sol did not eat. It seemed to him that eating was something a man did when he meant to go on as before. Pell took the trays away full and said nothing about it, and once, when Sol had drunk nothing since the packet, he sat on the edge of the bed and held the cup to Sol’s mouth with his own hand, as if Sol were a child. Pell’s hand was perfectly steady.
“Thank you, Deacon.”
“Of course, Your Grace.”
Neither of them spoke of the packet. It lay between them like something spilled that both had agreed not to see.
At night, when the residence was quiet, he took the books out from under his pillow.

He could not read them. He opened them anyway, and turned them toward the window by habit. The old one was soft and loose in its binding and smelled of dust and something sweeter underneath, like dried flowers. When he turned a page, the corner came away in his fingers, and he sat very still, horrified, and then laid the fragment back where he thought it had come from, as though that would help. After that he only held it.

The other was Stephen’s, cheap and stiff, its pages covered from edge to edge. The pen had been pressed hard, and the letters stood up in the paper like the faintest braille, and he ran his fingers over them again and again in the dark, as if the shapes might come through his skin if he were patient enough. They never did. Somewhere in those pages, he supposed, was the word the voice had said to him. He could not find it. He held the book open against his chest and felt the writing press against his shirt, and the notice glowed in the corner of the dark. Renewal. Three days.

Once that first night, without deciding to, he felt his way along the wall to the chest where his stoles were kept, and reached to the back of the drawer, and his fingers closed on the little steel rule as if they had gone there on an errand. He ran his thumb down it in the dark and found that he was counting off the marks, the long and the short, as surely as if he could see them. He could not read a word of Stephen’s book. He could read this. He could not think what he had ever measured with it, and he put it back where it lived and went back to bed.
On the second day he began to remember Stephen properly.

Not the claims. The man. The way he had sat on the edge of his bed in the cell on Serenity with his hands loose between his knees, because his back hurt him if he sat up straight. The way he laughed at his own jokes before he had finished telling them, a short dry breath through the nose. The way he had said Sol every time, never Your Grace, never Bishop, as if he were reminding him of something. How tired he had been, and how unafraid. How at the very end, with the wardens’ calm hands on him, he had not looked at the wardens at all. He had looked at Sol. And he had said it with what breath he had left, not to Sol but past him, to someone Sol could not see: Do not hold this against him.
Sol lay with that in the dark, and something in his chest began to tighten.

He thought for a moment it was another seizure, and waited for the old warning behind his eye. This came from lower down. It rose from under his ribs and closed his throat, and his breath began to come in pieces, short and broken, and his face did something he had not asked it to do, and a sound came out of him that he had never heard a man make.
Then his face was wet.

He touched it, and thought at first that it was blood, that he had bitten his tongue again, and he could not see his fingers to know. But it was not blood. It ran from his eyes, from his blind eyes, down his temples into his hair, and it would not stop, and the sound would not stop either, and he turned on his side and pressed his face into the pillow and wept for Stephen Hale.

Everyone he had ever comforted had someone in the City. He had never had anyone there, and had called it luck. Now he had lost someone, and he had signed him through the door himself, believing he was sending him up. No Pearl in all the worlds would ever show him that tired, amused face again. There was no City for Stephen. There was a door at the back of a white room, and reclamation, and the dark sea under the ice, and a gate that had not opened.
Unless the old man had seen something else, at the very end, looking up past all of them. Oh. Look. It’s open. Sol held on to that in the dark, and did not know whether he was allowed to.

At his temple the Halo warmed. He felt it come, the old slow warmth that had met him at every Pearl of his life, spreading down into his neck and shoulders, feeling for the place where the grief was, as it must have felt for Rena Arden’s by a cot on Serenity. It did not find it. It spread, and searched, and could get no grip on whatever had hold of him now, and after a while it cooled and went still, and he went on weeping.

He knew what he was doing. He had preached against it all his life. There shall be no more mourning, nor crying. Grief was the oldest rebellion, the refusal of the gift, a man setting his own sorrow above the mercy that had wiped it away. It was blasphemy. He was a bishop of Life, and he lay in his own bed in the residence at Concord and committed it, and did not stop.

He wept for Stephen, and then for the line of faces in the white light, whose names he did not know, and for the families on every world who knelt each evening to a soft light and laid a place beside it. He wept for Pell, who had never been unhappy. He had thought that Renewal had taken the capacity out of him, the way it took everything else. It had not. It had only been waiting.
The door opened.
“Your Grace?” Pell’s voice, close and frightened. “Your Grace, are you in pain?”
“Yes,” Sol said into the pillow.

Pell did not move. Sol could hear him breathing in the doorway, quick and shallow. Pell had seen the archive images, everyone had: the faces of the first world, twisted, wet, mouths open. He had never in his life seen a living man do it.
“Your face,” Pell said. His voice had gone very small. “Your Grace, your face...”
“I know.”
A long silence. Then, because Pell was Pell and could not do otherwise, he said, “Yes, Your Grace,” and went out, and closed the door softly behind him.

That night Sol dreamed for the first time since the packet. He dreamed of a big man coming through a door. He could not see the man’s face, only the size of him, the shoulders filling the frame, and his hands, which were very large and wet, as if he had just been washing them. The man did not say anything. He only came in, and stood there with his wet hands, and waited. Sol woke with his heart pounding, and the notice was in the corner of the dark. Renewal. Two days.
On the afternoon of the third day, Pell knocked.
“Your Grace. There’s a man at the door.”
“I’m seeing no one.”

“I told him so. He won’t go. He’s...” Pell paused. “He’s a dockworker, Your Grace. From Titan, he says. Off the Thorne freighters. He’s been standing in the side court for an hour. The housekeeper wanted to call the Mercy Office, he’s so odd.” Another pause. “He asked for you by name, Your Grace. By your first name. He asked for Sol.”
Sol sat up.
“Let him in.”
“Your Grace...”
“Let him in, Pell.”

He heard the man before he could have seen him, if he could have seen. The floor took his weight differently. He came in and stopped just inside the door, and he smelled of cold and machine oil and something sharp underneath, like fuel. He breathed heavily, the way large men breathe. He did not come any closer.
“You’re him,” the man said. His voice was deep and rough and very quiet. “The bishop.”
“Yes.”
“I know who you are. I know what you did.” He swallowed. Sol heard it. “You signed for Stephen. In Abundance. Everybody knows. You put your name on him and they took him to Serenity.”
“Yes.”
“I want you to know, if this is a trap, I came anyway.” The man let out a long breath. “I’m Tobin. Tobin Marsh. I work the docks at Plenty.”
“Why did you come?”

Tobin was quiet for a moment. When he spoke again, he sounded almost embarrassed. “I’m not a dreaming man. Never have been. I sleep like a dead thing. But three nights ago somebody said my name. Right there in the bunkroom, clear as you. Said get up and go to Concord, to the bishop’s house on the long straight street with the pillars, and ask for Sol. Said you were blind. Said you’d been shown me coming, so you’d know me.” He shifted his weight. “I said, that’s the one who took Stephen. That’s the one. And he said, I know. Go anyway. He’s mine now.”
Sol sat on the edge of his bed with his hands on his knees and his blind eyes turned toward the voice.
“Your hands,” he said. “Have you been washing your hands?”
A pause. “In the court fountain. They were filthy off the freighter. I didn’t want to come in like that.” Then, more slowly: “How’d you know that?”
Sol did not answer. He could not.
“You knew him,” he said instead. “Stephen.”

“He stayed with me on Plenty, a while. Before he went to Mars.” Tobin’s voice changed. “He said he had to find somebody. I told him not to go. He went anyway. He was like that.” A breath. “Is he in Mercy?”

He could have said yes. It was what everyone said. It was what Sol had said to a hundred families, gently, with his hand on their shoulders. Your husband is in Mercy. Your daughter is resting. She can’t receive yet.
“He’s dead,” Sol said. “I was there. I watched them do it.”

Tobin made a sound. It was the sound Sol had made the night before, the same breaking in the breath, but it came out of the big man without any shame at all, the way rain comes out of a sky. Sol listened to him weep. He had never heard anyone else do it. It did not sound like rebellion. It sounded like love with nowhere left to go.
“He prayed for me,” Sol said, when he could. “At the end. He asked that it not be held against me.”

Tobin wiped his face. Sol heard the rasp of a sleeve. “Well,” he said thickly. “That’s Stephen.” And then, after a while, with something in his voice that Sol thought it must have cost him a great deal to find: “Then I guess I’d better too.”
He came across the room. Sol felt the bed shift as Tobin knelt in front of him, and then two hands, enormous and still cold from the fountain, closed gently over his eyes.

“Brother Sol,” Tobin said. “The one you met on the way sent me. So you can see again, and so you can have the Spirit.” He hesitated, and then he prayed, plainly, as if he were talking to a foreman he trusted. “Lord, you said. So here I am. Here he is.”

Something moved under the hands. It was like grit, or ash. Sol felt it come away from his eyes in flakes, dry and light, the way the corner of the old book had come away in his fingers, and Tobin took his hands back, and the light came in.

It hurt. It was only the ordinary afternoon light of his own room, the filtered amber of Ganymede’s dome, but it struck him like a blow and he cried out and covered his face. Then, slowly, he lowered his hands.

There was a man kneeling in front of him. He was very big, with a broad plain face and a nose that had been broken once and never properly set, and small lines at the corners of his eyes, and the eyes themselves red and swollen and wet. His jacket said THORNE across the chest in faded letters. His hands rested on his knees, scrubbed raw. He was looking at Sol with an expression Sol had seen only once before, in a market on Mars, over a basket of spilled saffron.
“There you are,” Tobin said.

Sol looked at him for a long time. Then he looked at the room: the tall window, the untouched tray, the white Book of Life lying face down on the floor where he had dropped it three nights ago. He opened Stephen’s notebook and saw the handwriting at last, small and dense and slanting, running to every edge of the page.
“What do I do now?” he said.
Tobin got up off his knees and looked at the washstand in the corner, with its basin and its tall silver ewer. He lifted the ewer and weighed it in his hand, and found it full.
“Why wait?” he said. “Get up and be washed.”
Sol stood. His legs were weak from three days in bed. “Will it change anything,” he said, “if I don’t...” He did not know how to finish.

“If you don’t mean it? No.” Tobin’s voice was very simple. “Nothing happens. I’ve seen men try it, scared of dying, wanting a way out. Water’s just water then.” He set the basin on the floor. “Get down. Tell him. Not me. Tell him what you did.”

Sol knelt on the carpet with the basin in front of him. For a moment he could not find anything to say. Then it came, all of it, the way the weeping had come, from somewhere under his ribs. He told it to the empty air of his room. He told it the custody forms and how easily he had signed them. He told it the families he had comforted with lies he had believed. He told it Mercy Hall, and how he had stood at the glass and been moved, and called it holy, and signed. He told it the market and the packet and the white light. He told it Stephen. He told it all the names he could remember, and when he ran out of names, he told it that there were more, many more, and that he did not know them, and that he was sorry, and that sorry was not enough, and that he knew it was not enough.
When he stopped, the notice was there in the corner of his sight, small and gold and patient, as it had been for three days. Renewal. Tomorrow.

Tobin saw his eyes go to it. “That goes out when the water’s on you,” he said. “It won’t come back. And then the years come for you, all the ones it’s been holding off. You saw what they did to Stephen.”
“I saw.”

Tomorrow, at the morning office, there was a chair and a hood, and he would wake lighter, as he had always woken, and none of this would have happened to him. He looked at the small gold word until it was only a word.
He said the name anyway.

He said it aloud, in his own voice, in a bishop’s residence in the church’s own city, and it was the first time anyone had ever said it in that house. Christ. It did not sound like a word. It sounded like someone answering a door.
Tobin poured the water.

It was cold. It ran over his head and down his neck and soaked the collar of his shirt and dripped from his nose into the basin. Tobin poured it three times, and said with each pouring, in the careful voice of a man who has learned something by heart and is afraid of getting it wrong, “In the name of the Father. And of the Son. And of the Holy Spirit.” Then, more quietly: “Stephen taught me the words. I’ve only done it twice.”
Sol knelt with the water running off him, and he heard the hum stop.

He had never known it was there. That was the strangest thing, afterward. It had been there since the day he was born, beneath every sound and every silence, so constant that it was not a sound at all but the floor that sounds stood on, faint and warm and endless in the bones of his skull. And now it was not.

It did not fade. It simply ended, as a held note ends when the singer runs out of breath, and in the place where it had been there was a silence so total and so sudden that he put both hands flat on the floor, as if the floor might tilt. The gold notice in the corner of his sight flickered. Renewal. To... and went out. The little lights that had always lived at the edge of his vision, so faint he had never looked at them directly, went out too, one by one, like windows in a city going dark.

He was afraid. He was more afraid than he had ever been, more than in the white light, more than in the blindness. He was alone in his own head for the first time in his life, and he did not know how big it was in there, or whether there was anything in it but him.
And then, slowly, he understood that he was not alone.

It was not a hum. It was nothing he could hear. It was more like the quiet of the white light, that light that had seen all the way through him and burned and held him anyway. It did not press. It did not ask for anything. It was simply there, the way the floor was there under his hands.
“It’s gone, isn’t it,” Tobin said softly. “The hum.”
“Yes.”
“Takes some getting used to.” Tobin crouched beside him. “Talk to him. That’s all it is. Just talk.”

Sol did not know how. He had prayed every day of his life, before every Pearl, and every prayer had been a request. He opened his mouth to ask for something and found there was nothing he wanted to ask.

“I don’t know you,” he said at last. His voice cracked. “I hunted you. I didn’t know I was doing it, and I did it anyway. I signed for your people. I signed for Stephen. He asked you not to hold it against me. Please. Please don’t.” He stopped. Water dripped from his chin. “And if he’s with you, tell him... tell him I came. Tell him it was me.”
That was all. It did not seem like enough. He stayed on his knees anyway, with his wet hands on the carpet, and did not get up.
A sound came from the doorway.

Pell stood there with a tray in his hands. Sol did not know how long he had been there. The tray held a pot of tea and a covered dish, and it was tilting slowly in his grip, and the cup was sliding toward the edge. Pell’s eyes went from the basin, to the water darkening the carpet, to the dockworker crouched on the floor, to the bishop of Life on his knees with his hair dripping, looking straight back at him with eyes that could see.
The cup reached the edge of the tray, and fell, and broke.

Pell did not look down at it. His face was doing something Sol had never seen it do in sixty years, something it did not seem to know how to do, as though every muscle in it were reaching for an expression it had never been given.
